raw: CHAPTER XVII. One Night
en: [Chapter 17] One Night

raw: Never did the sun go down with a brighter glory on the quiet corner in Soho, than one memorable evening when the Doctor and his daughter sat under the plane-tree together.
en: The sun never set with a brighter glory on the quiet corner in Soho than one memorable evening when the Doctor and his daughter sat together under the plane tree.

raw: Never did the moon rise with a milder radiance over great London, than on that night when it found them still seated under the tree, and shone upon their faces through its leaves.
en: The moon never rose with a softer light over London than on that night, shining on their faces through the leaves.

raw: Lucie was to be married to-morrow.
en: Lucie was to be married the next day.

raw: She had reserved this last evening for her father, and they sat alone under the plane-tree.
en: She had reserved this last evening for her father, and they sat alone under the tree.

raw: “You are happy, my dear father?”
en: "Are you happy, my dear father?"

raw: “Quite, my child.”
en: "Quite, my child."

raw: They had said little, though they had been there a long time.
en: They had said very little, though they had been sitting there a long time.

raw: When it was yet light enough to work and read, she had neither engaged herself in her usual work, nor had she read to him.
en: When it was still light enough to read and work, she had done neither.

raw: She had employed herself in both ways, at his side under the tree, many and many a time; but, this time was not quite like any other, and nothing could make it so.
en: Usually, she sat by his side under the tree working or reading to him, but this evening was different from any other.

raw: “And I am very happy to-night, dear father.
en: "I am very happy tonight, dear father.

raw: I am deeply happy in the love that Heaven has so blessed--my love for Charles, and Charles’s love for me.
en: I am deeply happy in my love for Charles, and Charles’s love for me.

raw: But, if my life were not to be still consecrated to you, or if my marriage were so arranged as that it would part us, even by the length of a few of these streets, I should be more unhappy and self-reproachful now than I can tell you.
en: But if my life were not still dedicated to you, or if my marriage separated us, even by a few streets, I would be very unhappy.

raw: Even as it is--”
en: Even as it is, "

raw: Even as it was, she could not command her voice.
en: Her voice faltered, and she could not finish.

raw: In the sad moonlight, she clasped him by the neck, and laid her face upon his breast.
en: In the soft moonlight, she hugged him by the neck and rested her face on his chest.

raw: In the moonlight which is always sad, as the light of the sun itself is--as the light called human life is--at its coming and its going.
en: They sat in the moonlight, which always feels a little sad, like human life itself.

raw: “Dearest dear!
en: "Dearest father!

raw: Can you tell me, this last time, that you feel quite, quite sure, no new affections of mine, and no new duties of mine, will ever interpose between us? _I_ know it well, but do you know it?
en: Can you tell me, this last time, that you are sure my new love and duties will never stand between us?

raw: In your own heart, do you feel quite certain?”
en: I know it, but do you know it in your heart?"

raw: Her father answered, with a cheerful firmness of conviction he could scarcely have assumed, “Quite sure, my darling! More than that,” he added, as he tenderly kissed her: “my future is far brighter, Lucie, seen through your marriage, than it could have been--nay, than it ever was--without it.”
en: Her father answered with a firm, cheerful conviction: "I am quite sure, my darling!" He kissed her tenderly and added, "More than that, my future looks much brighter, Lucie, because of your marriage than it ever did without it."

raw: “If I could hope _that_, my father!--”
en: "If I could only hope that, father!"

raw: “Believe it, love!
en: "Believe it, my love!

raw: Indeed it is so.
en: Indeed it is true.

raw: Consider how natural and how plain it is, my dear, that it should be so.
en: Consider how natural and how plain it is, my dear, that things should be this way.

raw: You, devoted and young, cannot fully appreciate the anxiety I have felt that your life should not be wasted--”
en: You are young, and you cannot fully understand how much I worried that your life would be wasted, "

raw: She moved her hand towards his lips, but he took it in his, and repeated the word.
en: She put her hand to his lips to stop him, but he took her hand and repeated the word.

raw: “--wasted, my child--should not be wasted, struck aside from the natural order of things--for my sake.
en: ", wasted, my child, for my sake. Your unselfishness prevents you from seeing how much I thought about this.

raw: Your unselfishness cannot entirely comprehend how much my mind has gone on this; but, only ask yourself, how could my happiness be perfect, while yours was incomplete?”
en: But ask yourself: how could I be perfectly happy if your happiness was incomplete?"

raw: “If I had never seen Charles, my father, I should have been quite happy with you.”
en: "If I had never met Charles, father, I would have been perfectly happy with you."

raw: He smiled at her unconscious admission that she would have been unhappy without Charles, having seen him; and replied:
en: He smiled at her admission that she would be unhappy without Charles now that she had met him, and replied:

raw: “My child, you did see him, and it is Charles.
en: "My child, you did meet him.

raw: If it had not been Charles, it would have been another.
en: If it hadn't been Charles, it would have been someone else.

raw: Or, if it had been no other, I should have been the cause, and then the dark part of my life would have cast its shadow beyond myself, and would have fallen on you.”
en: Or if you had never married, I would have been the cause, and the shadow of my past imprisonment would have ruined your life too."

raw: It was the first time, except at the trial, of her ever hearing him refer to the period of his suffering.
en: It was the first time, other than at the trial, that she had heard him speak of his time in prison.

raw: It gave her a strange and new sensation while his words were in her ears; and she remembered it long afterwards.
en: Hearing his words gave her a strange feeling, which she remembered long afterward.

raw: “See!” said the Doctor of Beauvais, raising his hand towards the moon. “I have looked at her from my prison-window, when I could not bear her light.
en: "Look!" said the Doctor, pointing toward the moon. "I watched the moon from my prison window when I couldn't bear its light.

raw: I have looked at her when it has been such torture to me to think of her shining upon what I had lost, that I have beaten my head against my prison-walls.
en: I watched it when it was torture to think of it shining on everything I had lost, and I beat my head against the prison walls.

raw: I have looked at her, in a state so dull and lethargic, that I have thought of nothing but the number of horizontal lines I could draw across her at the full, and the number of perpendicular lines with which I could intersect them.” He added in his inward and pondering manner, as he looked at the moon, “It was twenty either way, I remember, and the twentieth was difficult to squeeze in.”
en: I watched it when I was so numb and depressed that I could only count the lines I could draw across it. I remember there were twenty lines either way, and the twentieth was hard to squeeze in."

raw: The strange thrill with which she heard him go back to that time, deepened as he dwelt upon it; but, there was nothing to shock her in the manner of his reference.
en: The strange feeling she had hearing him talk of his prison years deepened as he continued, though his tone was calm.

raw: He only seemed to contrast his present cheerfulness and felicity with the dire endurance that was over.
en: He was simply contrasting his present happiness with his past suffering.

raw: “I have looked at her, speculating thousands of times upon the unborn child from whom I had been rent.
en: "I watched the moon, wondering thousands of times about the child I had been torn from.

raw: Whether it was alive.
en: I wondered if it was alive, or if the shock had killed its mother.

raw: Whether it had been born alive, or the poor mother’s shock had killed it.
en: I wondered if it was a son who would one day avenge me.

raw: Whether it was a son who would some day avenge his father. (There was a time in my imprisonment, when my desire for vengeance was unbearable.) Whether it was a son who would never know his father’s story; who might even live to weigh the possibility of his father’s having disappeared of his own will and act.
en: There was a time when my desire for vengeance was unbearable. I wondered if it was a son who would never know my story, or might believe I had disappeared on purpose.

raw: Whether it was a daughter who would grow to be a woman.”
en: Or if it was a daughter who would grow up to be a woman."

raw: She drew closer to him, and kissed his cheek and his hand.
en: She drew closer, kissing his cheek and hand.

raw: “I have pictured my daughter, to myself, as perfectly forgetful of me--rather, altogether ignorant of me, and unconscious of me.
en: "I imagined my daughter grew up completely ignorant of me.

raw: I have cast up the years of her age, year after year.
en: I counted her age, year after year.

raw: I have seen her married to a man who knew nothing of my fate.
en: I imagined her married to a man who knew nothing of my fate.

raw: I have altogether perished from the remembrance of the living, and in the next generation my place was a blank.”
en: I was entirely forgotten by the living, and my place in the family was a blank."

raw: “My father!
en: "My father!

raw: Even to hear that you had such thoughts of a daughter who never existed, strikes to my heart as if I had been that child.”
en: Even hearing that you had such thoughts makes my heart ache as if I had been that child."

raw: “You, Lucie?
en: "You, Lucie?

raw: It is out of the Consolation and restoration you have brought to me, that these remembrances arise, and pass between us and the moon on this last night.--What did I say just now?”
en: These memories only arise because of the healing and happiness you have brought me. We share them on this last night under the moon. What was I saying just now?"

raw: “She knew nothing of you. She cared nothing for you.”
en: "You said she knew nothing of you and did not care."

raw: “So!
en: "Yes.

raw: But on other moonlight nights, when the sadness and the silence have touched me in a different way--have affected me with something as like a sorrowful sense of peace, as any emotion that had pain for its foundations could--I have imagined her as coming to me in my cell, and leading me out into the freedom beyond the fortress.
en: But on other nights, when the silence brought a sad peace, I imagined her coming to my cell and leading me out to freedom. I saw her figure in the moonlight, just as I see you now, though I could never hold her.

raw: I have seen her image in the moonlight often, as I now see you; except that I never held her in my arms; it stood between the little grated window and the door.
en: I have often seen her image in the moonlight, just as I see you now, except that I never held her in my arms; the image stood between the small barred window and the door.

raw: But, you understand that that was not the child I am speaking of?”
en: But you understand that was not the child I am speaking of?"

raw: “The figure was not; the--the--image; the fancy?”
en: "The image was not the real child, but a fancy?"

raw: “No. That was another thing.
en: "No, that was a phantom.

raw: It stood before my disturbed sense of sight, but it never moved.
en: The child my mind pursued was more real.

raw: The phantom that my mind pursued, was another and more real child.
en: I only knew she looked like her mother.

raw: Of her outward appearance I know no more than that she was like her mother. The other had that likeness too--as you have--but was not the same.
en: The phantom looked like her mother too, as you do, but it was different.

raw: Can you follow me, Lucie?
en: Can you follow me, Lucie?

raw: Hardly, I think?
en: Probably not.

raw: I doubt you must have been a solitary prisoner to understand these perplexed distinctions.”
en: I think only a prisoner could understand these strange distinctions."

raw: His collected and calm manner could not prevent her blood from running cold, as he thus tried to anatomise his old condition.
en: His calm manner did not stop her from feeling a chill as he analyzed his old state of mind.

raw: “In that more peaceful state, I have imagined her, in the moonlight, coming to me and taking me out to show me that the home of her married life was full of her loving remembrance of her lost father.
en: "In that peaceful state, I imagined her leading me out to show me her married home, which was full of loving memories of her lost father.

raw: My picture was in her room, and I was in her prayers.
en: My picture was on her wall, and I was in her prayers.

raw: Her life was active, cheerful, useful; but my poor history pervaded it all.”
en: Her life was active and happy, but my story was part of it."

raw: “I was that child, my father, I was not half so good, but in my love that was I.”
en: "I was that child, father. I was not nearly as good, but in my love, that was me."

raw: “And she showed me her children,” said the Doctor of Beauvais, “and they had heard of me, and had been taught to pity me.
en: The Doctor said, "And she showed me her children, who had been taught to pity me.

raw: When they passed a prison of the State, they kept far from its frowning walls, and looked up at its bars, and spoke in whispers.
en: When they passed a state prison, they looked at the bars and spoke in whispers.

raw: She could never deliver me; I imagined that she always brought me back after showing me such things.
en: She could never rescue me; I imagined she always brought me back to my cell afterward.

raw: But then, blessed with the relief of tears, I fell upon my knees, and blessed her.”
en: But then, relieved by tears, I knelt and blessed her."

raw: “I am that child, I hope, my father.
en: "I am that child, father.

raw: O my dear, my dear, will you bless me as fervently to-morrow?”
en: I hope you will bless me just as warmly tomorrow."

raw: “Lucie, I recall these old troubles in the reason that I have to-night for loving you better than words can tell, and thanking God for my great happiness.
en: "Lucie, I remember these old troubles tonight only because they show how much I love you and how grateful I am to God.

raw: My thoughts, when they were wildest, never rose near the happiness that I have known with you, and that we have before us.”
en: My wildest thoughts in prison never imagined the happiness I have found with you, and what lies ahead for us."

raw: He embraced her, solemnly commended her to Heaven, and humbly thanked Heaven for having bestowed her on him.
en: He hugged her, blessed her, and thanked God for giving her to him.

raw: By-and-bye, they went into the house.
en: After a while, they went inside.

raw: There was no one bidden to the marriage but Mr.
en: No one was invited to the wedding except Mr.

raw: Lorry; there was even to be no bridesmaid but the gaunt Miss Pross.
en: Lorry, and Miss Pross was the only bridesmaid.

raw: The marriage was to make no change in their place of residence; they had been able to extend it, by taking to themselves the upper rooms formerly belonging to the apocryphal invisible lodger, and they desired nothing more.
en: The marriage would not change where they lived. They had simply rented the upper rooms formerly belonging to the invisible lodger, and needed nothing more.

raw: Doctor Manette was very cheerful at the little supper.
en: Doctor Manette was very cheerful at dinner.

raw: They were only three at table, and Miss Pross made the third.
en: Only the three of them sat at the table: the Doctor, Lucie, and Miss Pross.

raw: He regretted that Charles was not there; was more than half disposed to object to the loving little plot that kept him away; and drank to him affectionately.
en: He regretted that Charles was not there, joking about the custom that kept him away, and drank a toast to him.

raw: So, the time came for him to bid Lucie good night, and they separated.
en: Finally, it was time to say good night, and they went to bed.

raw: But, in the stillness of the third hour of the morning, Lucie came downstairs again, and stole into his room; not free from unshaped fears, beforehand.
en: But in the quiet hours of the morning, Lucie came downstairs and crept into his room, feeling a sudden fear.

raw: All things, however, were in their places; all was quiet; and he lay asleep, his white hair picturesque on the untroubled pillow, and his hands lying quiet on the coverlet.
en: However, everything was in its place and quiet. He lay asleep, his white hair neat on the pillow, and his hands still.

raw: She put her needless candle in the shadow at a distance, crept up to his bed, and put her lips to his; then, leaned over him, and looked at him.
en: She put her unneeded candle in the shadows far away, crept up to his bed, and put her lips to his; then, she leaned over him, and looked at him.

raw: Into his handsome face, the bitter waters of captivity had worn; but, he covered up their tracks with a determination so strong, that he held the mastery of them even in his sleep.
en: His face still showed the worn lines of his long imprisonment, but he controlled his expressions even in his sleep.

raw: A more remarkable face in its quiet, resolute, and guarded struggle with an unseen assailant, was not to be beheld in all the wide dominions of sleep, that night.
en: A more remarkable face, in its quiet, determined, and guarded struggle with an unseen attacker, could not be found anywhere else in the wide world of sleep that night.

raw: She timidly laid her hand on his dear breast, and put up a prayer that she might ever be as true to him as her love aspired to be, and as his sorrows deserved.
en: She gently laid her hand on his chest, praying she would always be a good daughter to him.

raw: Then, she withdrew her hand, and kissed his lips once more, and went away.
en: Then she kissed him again and left.

raw: So, the sunrise came, and the shadows of the leaves of the plane-tree moved upon his face, as softly as her lips had moved in praying for him.
en: Soon the sun rose, and the shadows of the tree leaves moved softly across his face.
